title: Propagating failure without writing a match

prereqs.why: The whole problem is written so that every failure leaves the function through a ?, which is what makes the happy path a straight line.
You need to have written the explicit match version before the shorthand means anything.
Two of the failures start as a None from a slice lookup, and ? works on Option too.

statement:
Each line of input is a record: a `name`, then a `qty`. Parse each one, and
report what went wrong when it does not parse. Define your own error type:

```rust
enum RecordError {
    Missing(&'static str),    // a field was absent
    NotANumber(String),       // the qty was not an integer
    Negative(i64),            // the qty parsed but was below zero
}
```

with a `Display` impl printing, respectively, `missing <what>`,
`notanumber <token>` and `negative <value>`. Then write:

```rust
fn parse_record(fields: &[&str]) -> Result<(String, i64), RecordError>
fn second_word(line: &str) -> Option<&str>
```

Skip blank lines. For each non-blank line print two lines, then the totals:

```
ok <name> <qty>        or  err <the Display text of the error>
second <the second whitespace-separated word of the line, or none>
records <how many parsed>
errors <how many did not>
total <sum of the parsed quantities>
```

```
input:   bolt 5              output:  ok bolt 5
         nut                          second 5
         screw -2                     err missing qty
         washer x                     second none
                                      err negative -2
                                      second -2
                                      err notanumber x
                                      second x
                                      records 1
                                      errors 3
                                      total 5
```

Extra fields past the second are ignored - `bolt 5 spare` is a valid record.

### The point of the problem

`parse_record` can fail three ways, and the version you have already written in
the previous problem would be a staircase of `match`:

```rust
let name = match fields.first() {
    Some(n) => n,
    None => return Err(RecordError::Missing("name")),
};
let qty_tok = match fields.get(1) {
    Some(t) => t,
    None => return Err(RecordError::Missing("qty")),
};
let qty = match qty_tok.parse::<i64>() {
    Ok(v) => v,
    Err(_) => return Err(RecordError::NotANumber(qty_tok.to_string())),
};
```

Fifteen lines, of which three carry the logic. With `?` it becomes:

```rust
let name = fields.first().ok_or(RecordError::Missing("name"))?;
let qty_tok = fields.get(1).ok_or(RecordError::Missing("qty"))?;
let qty: i64 = qty_tok.parse().map_err(|_| RecordError::NotANumber((*qty_tok).to_string()))?;
```

`?` means: if this is an `Err` (or a `None`), return it from the enclosing
function now; otherwise give me the value inside. The failures are still
handled, still in the type, and still impossible to ignore - they are just no
longer the shape of the code.

`ok_or` turns an `Option` into a `Result` by supplying the error for the `None`
case, and `map_err` replaces one error type with another. Both exist because `?`
needs a `Result` whose error type matches the function's.

### `?` on an Option

`second_word` returns an `Option`, so `?` there propagates `None`:

```rust
fn second_word(line: &str) -> Option<&str> {
    let mut it = line.split_whitespace();
    it.next()?;        // no first word at all -> return None
    it.next()          // the second, which may also be None
}
```

`?` works in any function returning `Option` or `Result`, and the two cannot be
mixed - a `?` on an `Option` inside a function returning `Result` is a compile
error, which is what `ok_or` is for.

### Boundary cases

A line with no fields at all, which is skipped. A line with one field, giving
`missing qty` and `second none`. A qty of exactly 0, which is **not** negative
and so is valid. A negative qty, which parses and then fails the range check -
so the order of the two checks is observable. A qty that is not a number at all.
Extra fields, which are ignored. A line whose second word is not the qty of a
valid record - note `second` is computed from the raw line regardless of whether
the record parsed, so it prints something even for a failed line.

### Platform assumptions

Lines are at most 200 bytes, at most 200 of them, ASCII. Quantities that parse
fit in an `i64` and the valid ones sum to well inside 64 bits. A token too large
for an `i64` is reported as `notanumber`, because `parse` fails for it - the
error cause is collapsed deliberately, and the solution says what you would do
instead if the distinction mattered.
hints: `fields.first()` and `fields.get(1)` both return `Option<&&str>` - a reference to the element, which is itself a `&str`. That double reference is why the solution writes `(*name).to_string()`: dereference once to get the `&str`, then copy it into an owned `String`.

`ok_or(e)` turns `Some(v)` into `Ok(v)` and `None` into `Err(e)`, which is exactly the adapter `?` needs. Its sibling `ok_or_else(|| e)` only builds the error when it is actually needed - preferable when constructing it allocates.
Check `qty < 0` after the parse, with an explicit `return Err(...)`. Not every failure has to leave through a `?` - `?` is for propagating an error you were handed, and this one you are originating.

second 5
err missing qty
second none
err negative -2
second -2

second x
